scenes.visual: Title card: The cochlear amplifier. Subtitle: How active cells help us hear.

scenes.tts: The cochlear amplifier helps us hear weak sounds, separate nearby frequencies, and handle a wide range of loudness. It is an active process. In mammals, outer hair cells add energy to the vibration on each cycle of a sound. Their motor is a protein called prestin. A microphone in the ear canal can pick up sound that the cochlea sends back out. That sound gives us a way to check outer hair cell function.

scenes.visual: Lead with three benefit labels: detect weak sounds, separate nearby frequencies, handle a wide range of loudness. Show outer hair cells adding energy to a schematic vibration, with prestin labelled as their motor. End on a faint returning sound reaching an ear-canal microphone. Use qualitative schematics without numerical axes or a model of level-dependent gain.

scenes.tts: How does the cell add energy? Current through the transduction channel sets the voltage that drives prestin. Outer hair cells shorten and lengthen with voltage. Prestin responds directly, without burning A T P each cycle. In a prestin knock in mouse, transduction and cell mechanics were normal, yet amplification was lost. That is evidence that the cell body's motility is necessary for mammalian amplification.

Then show the prestin knock-in mouse result: normal transduction and cell mechanics, amplification lost. Remove the old cycle clock and speed-focused sequence.

scenes.tts: One electrical signature is nonlinear capacitance. In whole cell voltage clamp, a cell expressing prestin shows a bell shaped capacitance curve. The usual reading is voltage dependent charge movement in the protein. It does not measure the force or power a hair cell produces.

scenes.tts: Now listen to the returning sound. Otoacoustic emissions depend on the active process. A microphone in the sealed ear canal records them. These tests are used in newborn hearing screening. A pass shows that outer hair cell activity can produce an emission through the middle ear. It does not prove intact hearing. In auditory neuropathy, an emission can be normal while the auditory brainstem response is absent or very abnormal. The tests probe different stages.

scenes.visual: Move this scene after the prestin scenes. Keep the ear-canal microphone schematic, replacing the historical impulse traces and motor question mark with emission screening. Show outer hair cell activity and emission transmission through the middle ear. Beside it show the auditory nerve and brainstem-response test as a separate stage. Illustrate auditory neuropathy with emission present and brainstem response absent or very abnormal; never depict an emission pass as proof of intact hearing.

scenes.tts: In frogs, hair bundles can also add energy. Martin and Hudspeth studied excised adult bullfrog saccular tissue. A flexible probe moved individual bundles. The bundles dissipated more energy through fluid drag than the probe supplied. The extra energy came from the bundles themselves. A large movement alone would not show that: a passive bundle can move far on energy supplied by a probe. This does not show what bundles contribute in mammals.

scenes.visual: New scene labelled excised adult bullfrog sacculus. Show a flexible probe deflecting a hair bundle, then a qualitative energy balance: energy dissipated through drag exceeds energy supplied by the probe, with the bundle supplying the difference. Keep the frog preparation explicit. Do not depict this as a measured mammalian bundle contribution.

scenes.tts: The brain also sends input back to outer hair cells. Medial olivocochlear efferents release acetylcholine. Calcium entry activates nearby potassium channels. Acetylcholine shunts and hyperpolarizes the cells, suppressing their motility. This feedback regulates the cochlear amplifier, the active process that helps us detect weak sounds and separate nearby frequencies.
